articles.title: Is It Really Rude to Leave a One-Star Review?
articles.content:
About 10 years ago, my husband and I loaded our kids into the car and drove to what was billed as a destination family resort with an indoor water park. The ads promised a magical, kid-friendly escape worth the drive. We booked it without a second thought. We should have had at least one second thought.
When we arrived, the parking lot was empty. Not “offseason quiet” empty— more like “the last guests left under mysterious circumstances and nobody came after them” empty. The lobby carpet was torn up in patches. The hallways were dim and echoey. And the indoor water park, advertised with glistening slides and splashing families, consisted of exactly one broken slide standing in an otherwise empty pool. My kids’ faces broke my heart. The concierge was pleasant enough. She advised us to just wander the halls and pick whatever room looked good to us. So we chose the least creepy option, pushed the bureau in front of the door before bed, and left first thing in the morning.
That day, I wrote the only one-star review I have ever left in my life. It was two pages long and included photos. I went with equal parts scathing and cautionary. A few months later, I went back to see if the hotel had responded. Instead, I found that it had permanently closed. Part of me wonders whether my review was the final nail in the coffin.
But was leaving it actually the right thing to do? I’ve been thinking about it ever since, because the etiquette of negative reviews is genuinely murky, and the stakes can be higher than most of us realize.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more etiquette, tech, holiday tips, fun facts, humor and travel all week long.
The most obvious argument for a negative review is that you were asked and the service was truly terrible. Every time you visit a business, Google, Yelp, Amazon and everyone else wants to know how it went. We’ve built an entire consumer infrastructure around the premise that honest feedback is valuable.
So staying silent when you have had a genuinely terrible experience seems, if anything, like failing your civic duty. There weren’t any reviews of the hotel when I booked our trip (which should have been my first red flag), and they would have been so useful. The data backs this up: 94% of consumers say a negative review has convinced them to avoid a business.
Reviews are how strangers protect one another. When a hotel advertises a water park and delivers one sad slide in a drained pool, that’s not a minor inconvenience—it’s actually a misrepresentation. Plus, honest negative reviews can benefit businesses. A consistent pattern of one-star complaints about cold food is information that the management can act on. Silence isn’t kindness; it’s useless.
OK, but … a single one-star review can also do lasting, disproportionate damage to a small business. Especially if it’s exaggerated (as can happen when you write in the heat of the moment). A landmark Harvard Business School study found that a one-star drop on Yelp translates to a 5% to 9% revenue loss. And industry estimates suggest it takes roughly 40 positive customer experiences to claw back the reputational damage of just one negative review. For a small business operating on thin margins, that revenue loss could represent payroll, rent and the owner’s ability to keep the lights on.
Also, many of the issues stem from circumstances that no individual employee created. One terrible visit, driven by a broken system or an understaffed night, may not represent the whole story. Leaving a permanent, public indictment based on a single bad day can feel less like accountability and more like collateral damage.
It’s also worth noting that online review culture has developed a genuinely ugly side that has nothing to do with honest consumer feedback and everything to do with online bullying.
In 2025, a James Beard–nominated San Francisco chef found his restaurant review-bombed into closure after a dispute with a TikToker went viral. Hundreds of thousands of people who had never set foot in his restaurant, never tasted his food, never interacted with a single member of his staff flooded his Google page with one-star reviews because an influencer told them to. His employees were laid off, he lost his livelihood and his restaurant closed. And that’s just one example of many.
This is not etiquette; this is bullying. And it is one of the worst things happening in online culture right now. A review is supposed to be your honest account of your own experience. The moment you leave a one-star review for a business you’ve never visited, you’re not holding anyone accountable. You are, however, weaponizing hate. A review platform is not a pitchfork, and treating it like one doesn’t make you an activist—it makes you incredibly rude.
Here’s what I’ve settled on: A one-star review is appropriate when the problem was systemic, significant and likely to happen to the next person. Not because your server was having a hard shift. Not because your food arrived slightly cold during a Saturday-night rush. When there is genuine misrepresentation involved or consistent, recurring failures, you are not being rude. And I will say that given this rubric, I’ve never left another one-star review.
If you’re going to leave a one-star review, there are a few practical rules. Be specific, not mean. Describe what happened rather than what you think of the person who served you. Don’t write it in the heat of your emotions. And before you post anything, consider calling the business directly. A surprising number of problems get resolved this way, and a business willing to make it right deserves the opportunity. If they don’t respond, you will feel considerably better about that one star. Leaving a one-star review is not inherently rude—but the bar should be meaningfully higher than “I was mildly inconvenienced on a Tuesday.”
My two-page review of the haunted water park hotel, with its empty pool and bureau-against-the-door energy? One hundred percent warranted. I regret nothing. If I saved even one family from driving three hours to stand in a dark lobby choosing a room like contestants on Squid Game, that was a public service.

articles.title: In Charleston, Arkansas, a Strong Sense of Community Inspires Residents to Speak Up and Make a Difference
articles.content:
在阿肯色州的查尔斯顿，当你驶近这座小城时，会看到开阔的农田和简朴的房屋，直到高速公路变成大街。如果你注意观察，可能会看到一个50多岁的男士穿着高可见度背心，手持抓取工具和垃圾袋，在街道上清理垃圾。他名叫帕克·米德（Parker Meador），并非市政雇员。他这么做只是因为他愿意，因为他热爱这座城镇，因为这让他为邻居服务时感到自豪。

当地房地产经纪人、长期居民莱西·弗拉纳根（Lacy Flanagan）说：“帕克是个了不起的人。大多数城里人都认识他，也欣赏他为清理城市所做的努力。”米德的志愿清洁工作始于去年八月的一次散步。当时他带着女儿加布里埃尔（Gabrielle）出门，发现路上有垃圾，于是两人清理了一些纸屑、罐头和其他杂物。

这让他感到愉快，第二天他又去清理，很快形成了每天两小时、每周七天的习惯。一年后，他躲过了蛇、火蚁、交通和黄蜂，共清理了大约900袋垃圾，覆盖学校、公园、体育场、溪流等各处。路人鸣笛致意，有人停下来道谢，甚至有人给他拥抱。

“这从来不是工作，”他说，“我非常享受。这是服务上帝和社区、发挥作用的好方法。”发挥作用一直是米德一生的挑战，他患有多种精神健康障碍。他说：“我的生活异常艰难。仅仅活着就需要每日努力。我难以在众人面前工作，因此以其他方式服务家庭和社区。”

查尔斯顿是米德努力的完美舞台。这座城市距离俄克拉荷马州边境仅30分钟车程，有着1200人的规模，大街上是家庭经营的店铺和简朴的砖砌法院。查尔斯顿提名人贝弗利·多森（Beverly Dotson）说：“尽管我们只是个小镇，但很开放包容。”

这座小城有一段引人瞩目的历史。1954年《布朗诉教育委员会》案判决后，查尔斯顿成为南方第一个完全废除种族隔离的学区，且涉及小学到高中所有年级。同年，比利特尔岩（Little Rock）的九名非裔学生在三年后才面对国民警卫队，而查尔斯顿则在当年悄然关闭了非裔学生学校，接收了11名学生进入主校，既无抵抗，亦无媒体关注。

现任校长米西·摩尔（Missy Moore）说：“当时的领导人有远见和智慧。他们后代仍是社区的一部分，仍致力于公平对待所有人。”72年前，查尔斯顿人实现了这一开创性壮举。今年，他们再次创造奇迹。

2024年末，阿肯色州政府突然宣布购买查尔斯顿附近的815英亩土地建造一座3000张床位的监狱。大多数查尔斯顿居民愤怒不已：该城人口不足3000人，该计划将严重消耗资源并永久改变城市。更糟的是，政府未征求当地意见。

由农民、蓝领工人、数字游牧民、教师和奇卡莫加族成员组成的“Gravel & Grit”草根联盟应运而生。他们迅速研究了项目细节，发现尽管州政府已购买土地，但建设资金仍需立法机构审批。经过激烈游说，他们让立法者意识到地址不合适：土壤多石、地下水位低、道路不足、劳动力短缺。计划于4月搁置。弗拉纳根同时是奇卡莫加族的氏族母亲，她说：“看到大家团结合作是件美妙的事。”

这个小城再次战胜了强大的对手，像大卫对抗歌利亚，全靠社区精神。米德将他的垃圾清理行动发展为“查尔斯顿正能量”运动，包括路标、传单、Facebook页面和T恤，旨在展示城市的积极面，提高对精神健康的认知，鼓励社区服务。

他说：“我们可以对他人产生巨大影响，无论是积极还是消极，取决于我们的选择。”
articles.summary:
As you approach the little city of Charleston, ­Arkansas, you’ll see wide-open farm fields and modest homes before the highway becomes Main Street. Keep a good eye out, and there’s a chance you’ll also see a 50-something fellow wearing a high-visibility vest with a reacher-­grabber tool in one hand and a trash bag in the other, collecting litter off the streets. His name is Parker Meador, and he is not a city employee. He keeps Charleston clean because he wants to, because he loves the place, because it makes him feel good to serve his neighbors.

“Parker is a fantastic human being,” says real estate agent and longtime resident Lacy Flanagan. “The majority of people here know him and love him for his efforts to clean up the town.” Meador started this work on an impulse one day last August while out walking with his daughter Gabrielle. He noticed a bit of trash lying around, so they filled a plastic bag with wrappers, cans and other debris.

It made him feel good, so he went out the next day and did the same thing, and soon it became a routine. Now, he logs about two hours every day, seven days a week. A year in, having dodged snakes, fire ants, traffic and wasps, he has collected around 900 bags of trash from all over—schools, parks, sports fields, streams, creeks. People honk and wave. Some stop to thank him. Some give him hugs.

“It’s never a job,” he says. “I enjoy it tremendously. It’s a great way to serve God and our community and be useful.” Feeling useful has been a lifelong struggle for Meador, who has several mental health disorders. “My life is incredibly difficult,” he says. “Just to stay alive is a daily effort. I have a very difficult time working in front of people, so I serve my family and community in other ways.”

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more of the Nicest Places in America, heartwarming stories, fun facts, humor, cleaning, travel and tech all week long. 

A legacy of change

Charleston is the perfect setting for Meador’s effort. Located just 30 minutes from the Oklahoma border, it’s literally a one-stoplight town, and its Main Street is dotted with mom-and-pop shops and a simple brick courthouse. “Even though we’re just a small town, we’re very open-minded,” says Beverly Dotson, who nominated Charleston.

The city might be tiny and obscure, but it has an impressive claim to fame. Its school district was the first in the post-Confederacy South to desegregate all 12 grades after Brown v. Board of Education was decided in 1954. That same year, three years before nine brave students faced down the National Guard just two hours away in Little Rock, Charleston quietly shuttered its small school for Black students and welcomed the 11 pupils to its main institution—without resistance, press or fanfare.

“The leaders at the time were extraordinary people who had a vision and the wisdom to make it happen,” says Missy Moore, the current school superintendent. “The descendants of the people who made that decision are still part of this community and still want the same thing. We want to do right by everyone.” It was 72 years ago that the people of Charleston pulled off that groundbreaking feat. This year, they managed to pull off another one.

The power of coming together

It began in late 2024, when the state of Arkansas abruptly announced that it had purchased 815 acres just outside Charleston to build a 3,000-bed prison. Most people in Charleston were furious: There aren’t even 3,000 people living in the city, and this plan would massively strain resources and change the city forever. Worse, nobody even bothered to consult them.

A grassroots coalition of farmers, blue-collar workers, digital nomads, educators and members of the Chickamauga Nation—called Gravel & Grit— sprang up. They quickly educated themselves about the details of the ­proposed project and learned that although the governor’s office had purchased the land, construction funding still depended on the legislature. Through intensive lobbying, they ­convinced lawmakers that the site’s shortcomings would cause enormous ­overruns: The soil was too rocky, the water table too low, the roads insufficient, the labor supply inadequate. The project was shelved in April. “It was really neat to see it all come together,” says Flanagan, who is also a clan mother with the Chickamauga Nation.

The tiny city had prevailed once again, a David against a mighty Goliath, all thanks to that pervasive community spirit that shows up even in small ways, like Meador’s. He’s spinning his trash-removal efforts into a movement he calls Charleston Positive, complete with yard signs, fliers, a Facebook page and T-shirts, to celebrate positive things going on in the city, raise awareness about mental health and encourage community service.

“We can have such a huge impact on others,” he says, “in negative or positive ways. It’s our choice.”

Why trust us

For more than 100 years, Reader’s Digest has been known for its heartwarming true stories and focus on community. In 2017, we launched the Nicest Places in America, an annual contest that honors kind, inspiring people making a difference in their hometowns. Readers send in nominations, and Reader’s Digest’s editorial team vets the entries and whittles them down with the help of a panel of judges. This year, the judges included Today’s Al Roker, Tuesdays with Morrie author Mitch Albom, author and podcast host Mónica Guzmán, StoryCorps CEO Sandra Clark, Today co-anchor Craig Melvin, and Molly Irani, the co-founder of Chai Pani Restaurant Group in Asheville, North Carolina, which was 2025’s Nicest Place in America. articles.title: Swanville, Minnesota, Made a Promise to Give Scholarships to Every Student—And Transformed Generations of Kids
articles.content:
When Brody Kircher stepped up to receive his high school diploma and head off to college, he knew that the people of Swanville, Minnesota, would have his back. The only question was exactly how many dollars they would put in his pocket.
“I expected maybe $4,000,” he says. But the actual amount Kircher received was much more than he guessed: $6,000. “This community really comes together,” he says. “They’re trying to make sure that everyone has a chance. We’re kind of spoiled, honestly. In a bigger place, they wouldn’t be able to do it for everybody.”
For graduates of Swanville High School, there’s never any suspense about who’ll get a scholarship: If you apply, you’ll get one. And in this tiny town deep in Minnesota farm country, where the class of 2026 numbered just 22 students, almost every senior applies.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more of the Nicest Places in America, heartwarming stories, fun facts, humor, cleaning, travel and tech all week long.
Known as Dollars for Scholars, what started as a modest effort to help local students has evolved into a deep-rooted institution that now gives away about $100,000 in scholarships a year. Recipients can use the money for almost anything: college, trade school or continuing life skills for special education students. The program is backed by a year-round fundraising effort that includes bingo games, poinsettia sales, and weekly “meat raffles,” where locals buy chances to fill their freezers.
“Spin the wheel, and if it lands on your number, you win some meat,” says Dollars for Scholars president Teresa Giese, who nominated Swanville. “It’s a social thing. People love it. When my friends and I lose, we say, ‘It’s for the kids.’ ”
So how small is Swanville? The 2020 census counted just 326 people. Founded in 1883 as a timber town, Swanville today is a farming community best known for soybeans and the production of turkeys.
Drive through and you’ll see a cluster of homes, small businesses, grain elevators and steel storage sheds. You’ll see a bar called Lucky’s Saloon and a restaurant called Patriots Cafe that serves breakfast and lunch. You’ll see a school, a church and a little dirt road that leads to a little town dock on a little lake. Then you’ll be back in the soybean fields, on your way to the next little town.
“People say, ‘Oh, I’m from a small town; we know everybody’s name.’ I say, ‘We’re so small, we know everybody’s middle name,’ ” says Chris Kircher, Brody’s father, who chairs Swanville’s school board and owns a sporting goods store. But “small” doesn’t mean struggling. Last year, Dollars for Scholars surpassed $1 million in money awarded. Nobody imagined that kind of sustained success when a few locals launched the program in 1987, hoping to keep enrollment up and prevent the school from losing students to larger neighboring school districts.
“I was one of the first people to get a scholarship. I got it in 1991. I got $103,” says Chris. “I went to the bank, and they gave me a $100 bill and three ones.” These days, most students get at least a few thousand, and this year’s top recipient got $7,000.
The financial base is an interest-generating endowment established years ago with a $100,000 donation from the local Lions Club and buttressed by annual fundraising. The program allows local donors to create personalized scholarships, often in memory of friends and family. Those contributions are matched by the main fund, so $250 from a donor becomes $500 for a student.
“People here aren’t rich. We don’t have a lot of money. But when we need it, we find it,” says the elder Kircher.
“There were times when we were concerned that we were going to lose our school. Now we’re adding classrooms,” says Stephenie Och, whose mother helped found Dollars for Scholars.
Her son Ethan Och graduated in 2016 and won $3,000 in scholarships. That helped him stay on track in his critical first year at the University of Minnesota, providing ready cash for pesky expenses like dorm fees and books. It wasn’t the first time that Swanville stepped up for him. Spinal muscular atrophy, a rare genetic condition, had put him in a wheelchair when he was a toddler. The Lions Club helped make his home wheelchair accessible. After he started school, the community passed a referendum to upgrade the building, adding ramps and other modifications.
“They needed to modernize—it was such an old building,” says Ethan. “So they saw my situation as an opportunity, not just for me but for other students too.” Ethan got a degree in aerospace engineering and mechanics, and today is a software engineer working for one of the nation’s leading defense contractors: “My dream job,” he says. He’s also funding scholarships of his own, including one that went to Brody Kircher.
And as for Brody, he’s off at the University of Minnesota’s Morris campus, playing wide receiver. He can easily see himself coming back to Swanville someday, he says, and would recommend the town to anyone. “I liked not being a stranger to anybody,” he says. “It’s easy to get to know people. They have faith in you. They have faith in everyone.”

When Brody Kircher stepped up to receive his high school diploma and head off to college, he knew that the people of Swanville, Minnesota, would have his back. The only question was exactly how many dollars they would put in his pocket.

“I expected maybe $4,000,” he says. But the actual amount Kircher received was much more than he guessed: $6,000. “This community really comes together,” he says. “They’re trying to make sure that everyone has a chance. We’re kind of spoiled, honestly. In a bigger place, they wouldn’t be able to do it for everybody.”

For graduates of Swanville High School, there’s never any suspense about who’ll get a scholarship: If you apply, you’ll get one. And in this tiny town deep in Minnesota farm country, where the class of 2026 numbered just 22 students, almost every senior applies.

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more of the Nicest Places in America, heartwarming stories, fun facts, humor, cleaning, travel and tech all week long.

The small town with a big heart

Known as Dollars for Scholars, what started as a modest effort to help local students has evolved into a deep-rooted institution that now gives away about $100,000 in scholarships a year. Recipients can use the money for almost anything: college, trade school or continuing life skills for special education students. The program is backed by a year-round fundraising effort that includes bingo games, poinsettia sales, and weekly “meat raffles,” where locals buy chances to fill their freezers.

“Spin the wheel, and if it lands on your number, you win some meat,” says Dollars for Scholars president Teresa Giese, who nominated Swanville. “It’s a social thing. People love it. When my friends and I lose, we say, ‘It’s for the kids.’ ”

So how small is Swanville? The 2020 census counted just 326 people. Founded in 1883 as a timber town, Swanville today is a farming community best known for soybeans and the production of turkeys.

Drive through and you’ll see a cluster of homes, small businesses, grain elevators and steel storage sheds. You’ll see a bar called Lucky’s Saloon and a restaurant called Patriots Cafe that serves breakfast and lunch. You’ll see a school, a church and a little dirt road that leads to a little town dock on a little lake. Then you’ll be back in the soybean fields, on your way to the next little town.

“People say, ‘Oh, I’m from a small town; we know everybody’s name.’ I say, ‘We’re so small, we know everybody’s middle name,’ ” says Chris Kircher, Brody’s father, who chairs Swanville’s school board and owns a sporting goods store. But “small” doesn’t mean struggling. Last year, Dollars for Scholars surpassed $1 million in money awarded. Nobody imagined that kind of sustained success when a few locals launched the program in 1987, hoping to keep enrollment up and prevent the school from losing students to larger neighboring school districts.

“I was one of the first people to get a scholarship. I got it in 1991. I got $103,” says Chris. “I went to the bank, and they gave me a $100 bill and three ones.” These days, most students get at least a few thousand, and this year’s top recipient got $7,000.

Launching the next generation of dreamers

The financial base is an interest-generating endowment established years ago with a $100,000 donation from the local Lions Club and buttressed by annual fundraising. The program allows local donors to create personalized scholarships, often in memory of friends and family. Those contributions are matched by the main fund, so $250 from a donor becomes $500 for a student.

“People here aren’t rich. We don’t have a lot of money. But when we need it, we find it,” says the elder Kircher.

“There were times when we were concerned that we were going to lose our school. Now we’re adding classrooms,” says Stephenie Och, whose mother helped found Dollars for Scholars.

Her son Ethan Och graduated in 2016 and won $3,000 in scholarships. That helped him stay on track in his critical first year at the University of Minnesota, providing ready cash for pesky expenses like dorm fees and books. It wasn’t the first time that Swanville stepped up for him. Spinal muscular atrophy, a rare genetic condition, had put him in a wheelchair when he was a toddler. The Lions Club helped make his home wheelchair accessible. After he started school, the community passed a referendum to upgrade the building, adding ramps and other modifications.

“They needed to modernize—it was such an old building,” says Ethan. “So they saw my situation as an opportunity, not just for me but for other students too.” Ethan got a degree in aerospace engineering and mechanics, and today is a software engineer working for one of the nation’s leading defense contractors: “My dream job,” he says. He’s also funding scholarships of his own, including one that went to Brody Kircher.

And as for Brody, he’s off at the University of Minnesota’s Morris campus, playing wide receiver. He can easily see himself coming back to Swanville someday, he says, and would recommend the town to anyone. “I liked not being a stranger to anybody,” he says. “It’s easy to get to know people. They have faith in you. They have faith in everyone.”

Why trust us

For more than 100 years, Reader’s Digest has been known for its heartwarming true stories and focus on community. In 2017, we launched the Nicest Places in America, an annual contest that honors kind, inspiring people making a difference in their hometowns. Readers send in nominations, and Reader’s Digest’s editorial team vets the entries and whittles them down with the help of a panel of judges. This year, the judges included Today’s Al Roker, Tuesdays with Morrie author Mitch Albom, author and podcast host Mónica Guzmán, StoryCorps CEO Sandra Clark, Today co-anchor Craig Melvin, and Molly Irani, the co-founder of Chai Pani Restaurant Group in Asheville, North Carolina, which was 2025’s Nicest Place in America. articles.title: Brace Yourself! You’re About to Get a Lot More Political Fundraising Emails Before the Midterms—Here’s Why and What to Do About It
articles.content:
在民主国家，选举是我们的集体声音——即使在这个特定的民主体制中，最响亮的声音似乎来自一群邮件营销人员。这种情况在今年中期选举季节（11月3日大选前）将尤为明显。请准备好你的删除按钮，因为它将要频繁使用了。

为什么？就在你以为邮箱已经无法再塞入更多你不想读的内容时，一家主要的邮件服务商最近推出了新的政治集资规则。可以确定的是，这些政治组织会充分利用这些新规。你的邮箱能容纳多少内容？请耐心等待。情况将变得更糟——但你可以采取一些行动来应对。继续阅读了解详情。

订阅《读者文摘》的Read Up新闻通讯，获取更多新闻、科技、幽默、旅行和趣闻。

谷歌最近推出了新的Gmail认证发件人计划，允许“合格的、经过验证的政治委员会”将“符合政策且无骚扰的邮件”直接发送到你的邮箱收件箱，绕过垃圾邮件过滤器。

该计划面向候选人、政党、政治行动委员会（PAC）和其他向联邦选举委员会（FEC）或其他选举机构登记的类似组织开放。要符合条件，政治发件人必须经过验证，从公共域名发送邮件，并确保垃圾邮件占其发送的总邮件量的比例低于0.3%。如果用户标记超过0.3%的邮件为垃圾邮件，发件人可能会被暂停七天或被移出该计划。

该政策于9月8日生效，因此新的现实已经开始。

谷歌可能允许增加政治集资的一个原因是减少其需要应对的诉讼数量。共和国全国委员会（RNC）在2022年起诉谷歌，指控其通过垃圾邮件过滤器“限流”其邮件营销活动。该案被驳回，但RNC提出了上诉。2026年1月，RNC再次败诉。

同样在2022年，RNC和共和党参议院及众议院竞选委员会向FEC提交了联合投诉，指控谷歌的垃圾邮件过滤器故意审查其信息。FEC驳回了该投诉。其他多年的诉讼和投诉也遭遇了同样的结果。

但回到最初的问题。由于公司没有做出重大公告，尚不清楚谷歌是否认为这是个好主意，至少在让Gmail用户满意方面。谷歌悄悄更新了其帮助中心网站以反映政策变更，这表明它预计用户不会对增加的邮件流量感到满意。

这也不是谷歌第一次尝试。2022年，该公司启动了一个试点计划，同样阻止政治邮件被筛选为垃圾邮件。根据Axios对数百条评论的审查，对FEC的评论一致为负面。

主要问题不在于垃圾邮件的数量，而在于发件人本身。在这个计划下经过验证并不告诉你任何关于筹资者的商业实践或你的资金将去向的信息。

“我在国会做了大量工作，打击欺骗性PAC的集资活动。”加州前民主党众议员凯蒂·波特在政策公布时告诉CNN，“他们说要帮助选举退伍军人，但当你看看资金去向时，99.99%的资金回到了政治顾问的口袋里。这并没有解决这个问题。”

另一个风险是骗子试图模仿合法的政治组织来筹集资金、收集你的数据或黑客你的账户。2021年，司法部（DOJ）起诉了三人，指控他们欺骗性地筹集了350万美元来自不知情的捐赠者。在2024年大选前夕，FBI警告称，有网络钓鱼骗局、商品“无发货”骗局和其他伪装成合法政治信件的欺诈活动。

你可以减少它们，但完全阻止它们的可能性不大。以下是四种选择。
articles.summary:
In a democracy, elections are our collective voice—even if, in our specific democracy, the loudest voices seem to be a bunch of email marketers. That’s going to be especially apparent this midterm season, which is well underway ahead of the Nov. 3 election. Warm up that delete finger, because it will be getting a workout.

Why? Well, just when you thought your inbox couldn’t get any more stuffed with stuff you don’t want to read, a major email carrier recently launched new fundraising rules for political groups. And you can be certain they will take advantage of them. How much can possibly fit into our already-at-capacity inboxes? Just you wait. Things are about to get way worse—but there is something you can do about it. Read on for the details.

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more news, tech, humor, travel and fun facts all week long.

Why are we about to get an avalanche of political fundraising emails?

Google recently launched a new Gmail Verified Sender Program, which will allow “eligible, verified political committees” to send “policy-compliant and non-abusive messages” straight to your email inbox, bypassing the spam filter.

The program is open to candidates, political parties, political action committees (PACs) and similar groups registered with the Federal Election Commission (FEC) or other election authorities. To qualify, political senders must be verified, send emails from a public domain and keep spam below 0.3% of the total number of email they send. If users mark more than 0.3% as spam when the emails come in, senders can get suspended for seven days or booted from the program.

The policy went into effect on Sept. 8, so the new reality is well underway.

Why did Google think this was a good idea?

One reason Google may have decided to allow increased political fundraising is to reduce the number of lawsuits it’s had to respond to. The Republican National Committee (RNC) sued Google in 2022 for “throttling” its email messaging campaigns with its spam filters. The case was dismissed, but the RNC appealed. In January 2026, the RNC lost again.

Also in 2022, the RNC and the Republican Senate and Congressional campaign committees filed a joint complaint with the FEC over Google’s spam filters, which they accused of intentionally censoring their messages. The FEC dismissed the complaint. Other lawsuits and complaints over the years have met similar fates.

But back to the original question. Given the lack of a big announcement by the company, it’s not clear that Google does think it’s a good idea, at least in terms of pleasing Gmail recipients. Google quietly updated its Help Center website to reflect the policy change, underscoring the idea that it anticipates users will not be happy with the increased email traffic.

And this isn’t the first time Google tried this. Back in 2022, the company launched a pilot program that also prevented political emails from being filtered as spam. Comments to the FEC were uniformly negative, according to a review of hundreds of them by Axios.

Aside from an overflowing inbox, are there any other potential dangers?

The main one has less to do with the volume of spam and more with the senders themselves. Being verified under this program doesn’t tell you anything about the fundraisers’ business practices or where your money will go.

“I did a lot of work in Congress to crack down on scam PACs that send you fundraising,” Katie Porter, a former Democratic congresswoman from California, told CNN when the policy became public. “They say they’re going to help elect veterans, but when you look at where the money goes, 99.99% of the money goes back into the pockets of political consultants. This doesn’t do anything to tackle that.”

Another risk is scammers trying to mimic a legitimate political group to solicit funds, harvest your data or hack your accounts. In 2021, the Department of Justice (DOJ) charged three people with fraudulently soliciting $3.5 million from unsuspecting givers. And just before the 2024 election, the FBI warned of phishing scams, merchandise “no-shipment” scams and other fraudulent activity masked as legitimate political correspondence.

Is there any way to stop the deluge of emails?

You can reduce them, but it’s unlikely you can stop them completely. Here are four options.

  • Click unsubscribe. Google recommends that senders offer a one-click unsubscribe button, so use it. You can also open the message and navigate to the unsubscribe options at the company’s website.
  • Create a filter. In the search bar at the top, click the “show search options” icon to show filters. Or click the box next to an unwanted email, then hit the three dots menu and select “filter messages like these.”
  • Mark the email as spam. If a company does not unsubscribe you, mark the emails as spam. Know that this will not unsubscribe you, but it will send the emails automatically to your spam inbox.
  • Block the sender. If you want nothing else from the sender at all, open the email, hit the three dots “more” menu and select “Block [sender].”

Sources:

  • Google: “Gmail Verified Sender Program eligibility & policies”
  • New York Times: “Google Just Made It Easier for Campaigns to Send You Fund-Raising Emails”
  • Fox News: “Gmail change may flood your inbox with political email”
  • Reuters: “US appeals court rejects RNC lawsuit claiming Google email spam filters harmed fundraising”
  • CNN: “FEC dismisses RNC complaint that Google’s spam filters were biased against conservatives”
  • CNN Transcripts: “The Story Is with Elex Michaelson, Aug. 19, 2026”
  • U.S. Election Assistance Commission: “Alert – Misleading Voter Registration Phishing Email”
  • DOJ: “Three Individuals Charged with $3.5 Million Scheme to Collect Contributions for Fraudulent Political Action Committees”
  • Axios: “Leave campaign emails in spam, FEC commenters demand”

articles.title: We Tried a Beginner’s Pottery Kit—And Now We Wanna Clay All Day
articles.content:
Time away from screens is absolutely essential, especially in the age of AI. That’s why the recent rise of analog hobbies has been nothing short of a miracle for my mental health. In fact, spending a few minutes with a mini coloring book or investing in a monthly book subscription is an easy way to boost dopamine during my downtime—no doomscrolling required.
But the best hobbies are those that require practice and patience. That’s where at-home pottery kit brand Pottd comes in. These clever at-home pottery kits come with almost everything you need to put together pots, paint mugs or make your bestie an incense burner. And the best part? You don’t need any experience with clay to craft cute pieces. Here’s my experience getting hooked on these all-inclusive kits.
Pinch pots, painted mugs and pressed clay coasters—oh, my! Pottd kits come with dozens of different projects that scratch that creative itch.
There are several kits on Pottd to choose from, which fall into two categories: painting and pottery. Painting kits come with premade items along with the paints to decorate them. Pottd offers dozens of kits that come with things like picture frames, mugs, beer glasses, coasters or vases—you name it.
The pottery kits bring additional choices. Pick from general creativity kits or opt for specific kits that cover things like biscuit-shaped coasters, candle holders, baby keepsakes, sculptural plants, games and more. There are also extras like molds and paints available à la carte.
I opted for a general kit with “retro” paint colors. Pack neatly inside the kit is nearly everything you’ll need to make several different pieces, including:
First, take everything out of the box and arrange it on a flat surface. Now is the perfect time to unfurl that junk mail or those local grocery mailers crowding in your mailbox—they make excellent protection for your table!
The Quick Start guide is a great resource when first setting up your pottery zone. It outlines any extras you might want that don’t come with your kit, such as additional tools. While I didn’t have a ruler or rolling pin on hand, I did take its advice to ensure I had a cup of water set up for smoothing and adding “slip” to the clay. I also grabbed a reusable paper towel to keep messes to a minimum.
Next, I highly recommend setting the mood. If you’re like me, that means adding some background noise and good, solid lighting. While you can absolutely make your pottery in silence, popping on a good podcast, audiobook, or your favorite album helps keep that creativity flowing.
The Quick Start guide also comes with several instruction cards covering projects like a trinket dish, pinch pot, incense burner, vase, draped dish, photo stand and plant pot. Reading through these cards is super helpful when you’re considering your first pieces!
For my first project, a pinch pot, I unpacked one of the clay packets and separated out 1/4 of the bag as instructed. The rest goes back into the sealed bag for future projects. I popped the instruction card into the cardboard holder and got started.
Overall, the instructions are detailed and perfect for newbies. They go over each step in an easy-to-follow format, leaving plenty of room for creative choices. I especially appreciated the continued reminders to use water and the included sponge to keep the clay surface nice and slick. This clay tends to crack when it’s dry, so keeping it moist while you work is crucial for a nice, smooth look.
After making my pinch pot, I caught the creativity bug and decided to crank out an incense burner and a draped dish. This time, I also had a clearer direction: I wanted to model them after my favorite noms—breakfast foods! Even after crafting a bacon-shaped incense burner, an egg-shaped dish and my little pinch pot, I still had about a third of my first bag of clay leftover. I didn’t even dip into my second bag, so each box can easily handle several projects.
The hardest part was waiting for the clay to dry, which took about 48 hours. After that, you must apply a base coat, which takes about 1-2 hours to dry. It’s important to ensure that pottery is completely dry before painting. Once dry, it was time to paint my pottery!
This is the fun part! Using the paints that come in the kit, it’s time to decorate your pottery. For the best results, Pottd recommends working in thin layers and waiting for each layer to dry before adding another. Now is the time to get creative with stripes, spots, murals or whatever inspires you.
I used a reference photo for my bacon incense burner, and I’m pretty pleased with how it turned out! While the kit didn’t come with a white paint for my egg whites, I opted for a baby blue color and think it turned out pretty darn cute. For my pot, I pursued a polka-dotted aesthetic.
Once the paint has dried completely, the final step is to give it a good glaze. This step is optional, but it gives the pottery a more finished look. Plus, the glaze protects the paint from scratches and adds slight water resistance, though it’s best to keep all pottery away from water for the best longevity. Skipping this step gives the pottery a more rustic look, should that be your preferred direction.
Once you begin making clay pieces from a Pottd kit, it’s quite an addictive hobby! I found myself thinking about my next project soon after finishing my first batch. And because each kit includes so much clay, I was able to make a few pieces to give to friends as gifts as well. Overall, Pottd kits are an easy way to try out a new hobby. I already have my eye on additional kits like the Paint a Tea Set kit and the overstuffed Super Bundle.
Pottd kits span tons of options, including pottery, picture holders and pretty tea sets!
Folks looking for an all-in-one kit that makes it easy to experiment will love how inclusive Pottd kits are. Plus, they make great gifts for creatives or date night activities for couples’ holidays like anniversaries and Valentine’s Day. The brand is always rolling out new kits and creative tools, so check out the Pottd website to see what’s currently trending!
